apps/vault.title: Vault
apps/vault.about:
The Bitwarden or Vaultwarden vault's items, found by typing

a desk accessory (Gitea #71): the Bitwarden or Vaultwarden vault's items, found by typing, and a password, a username or a TOTP code copied for a while. Unlocking, locking and syncing are the desktop's own (wm/vault.hibr), so the window, Control Panel > Passwords and every Terminal opened after an unlock agree on whether it is open.
apps/vault.author: Omar Sakka
apps/vault.name: vault

apps/contacts.title: Contacts
apps/contacts.about:
The people in your address books, kept offline from CardDAV

the people in your address books, kept on this machine from a CardDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a list down the left, searchable, and the person chosen on the right -- their emails, any of which writes them a message in Mail, their phones, address, organisation and note. n adds someone, e or enter edits, # or delete removes, / searches, j and k move, R syncs now.

Which servers are used is Control Panel > PIM, from the Servers list; each is kept under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER by lib/pimsync.hibr, run in the background -- the only thing that writes there. A change made here is made to the list at once and queued for the server, conditional on the copy it was read from; the next sync sends it. Mail reads the same copies to finish an address as it is typed.
apps/contacts.author: Omar Sakka
apps/contacts.name: contacts

apps/switchboard.title: Switchboard
apps/switchboard.about:
Watch a longwire switchboard: who is on it and who is ringing whom

a window on a longwire switchboard you run: how many nodes are on it, which of them are online, and who is ringing whom right now. It reads the switchboard's own worker through `lw`, once a second, and follows its event stream for the calls. It watches; it does not decide anything (a ring and a registration are the script's to answer, and the script has two seconds). It shows no address and no key: the worker does not give the registry any.

A call is shown while it is being set up and for a few seconds after, and then it is gone. Nothing here is written to disk, and the window keeps no list of past calls: that is what the switchboard promises (docs/SWITCHBOARD.md).
apps/switchboard.author: Omar Sakka
apps/switchboard.name: switchboard

apps/xscreen.title: X Screen
apps/xscreen.about:
X11 programs in windows of their own

X11 programs in windows (Gitea #290, #291): Firefox, GTK and Qt programs, and anything else that speaks X11, run on the desktop. Each window starts an Xvfb of its own, a virtual X server that draws the screen into a file it maps, and the xscr module maps the same file and puts the screen into the window -- as pixels where the terminal can place them, half blocks where it cannot. Keys, clicks, drags, the wheel and paste go to it through XTEST; the screen is drawn only when the server says it changed (DAMAGE), so an idle or hidden one costs nothing.

The programs are a list Control Panel > X Screen keeps -- a name, a command, how its window behaves and how it is drawn -- and each one is an entry under Applications > X Screen, opening a window titled for it and, once the program names its own window, `Name [its title]`. The app itself is hidden: an empty screen with nothing on it is nothing to choose.
apps/xscreen.author: Omar Sakka
apps/xscreen.name: xscreen

apps/files.about:
A file browser for the desktop, and a lister on its own.

apps/term.title: Terminal
apps/term.about:
A shell in a window, which is the last step of decision 0020.

The window manager hands this app a rectangle and some keys; the term module runs a program on a pseudo terminal, keeps a picture of its screen and paints that picture into the rectangle. What runs inside is a real program with a real terminal: it edits its own line, draws its own colours and does not know it is in a window.
apps/term.author: Omar Sakka

apps/calendar.title: Calendar
apps/calendar.about:
Your calendars, a month at a time, kept offline from CalDAV

your calendars, kept on this machine from a CalDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a month at a time, each day's events in it, and the chosen day's events listed underneath; or an agenda of what is coming. The arrows choose a day, n and p (or page down and up) change month, t comes back to today, a and m switch to the agenda and back, tab moves between the month and the day's list, c makes an event on the chosen day, enter makes one there or edits the one chosen in the list, # removes it, R syncs now.

The servers are Contacts' -- Control Panel > PIM -- and lib/pimsync.hibr keeps their calendars under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER: each event's file, and every occurrence from a year back to two years on, which this reads by date. A change made here is queued and sent at the next sync. Reminders go off whether or not a Calendar window is open: a ticker run after every frame looks for the next one and asks for the frame it is due in.
apps/calendar.author: Omar Sakka
apps/calendar.name: calendar

apps/stickies.title: Stickies
apps/stickies.about:
Notes stuck on the desktop, each its own colour

notes stuck on the desktop, as many as you like, each its own colour, each saved as you type. Launching Stickies opens every note there is (a first, empty one if there are none); the Note menu makes a new one, changes the colour, and deletes one. Closing a note only puts it away until Stickies is opened again -- it is still there.

The colours are the notes' own, not the theme's, the way a game's art is: a yellow note is yellow on every theme. Text wraps at the window's width, and the desktop's Edit menu works on it -- undo and redo, cut, copy, paste, select all.
apps/stickies.author: Omar Sakka
apps/stickies.name: stickies

apps/imgview.title: Image Viewer
apps/imgview.about: A picture in a window, drawn by the img module. Opens with a path (dt_launch imgview "$path", the same as any other app takes one through its own _open), or empty and waiting for one dropped onto it from a file browser -- there is no file-open dialog anywhere in this desktop, so a drop is the only way in short of already knowing the path.
apps/imgview.author: Omar Sakka
apps/imgview.name: imgview

apps/calc.title: Calculator
apps/calc.about:
A calculator for the desktop, and a program on its own.

Sourced by a session it is an app: the window manager finds calc_draw, calc_key and calc_click and calls those.  Run directly it evaluates its arguments and prints the answer, so it is useful without a desktop:
apps/calc.author: Omar Sakka

apps/puzzle.title: Puzzle
apps/puzzle.about:
The sliding tile puzzle, 15 numbered tiles and one gap in a 4x4 frame. Arrows move the gap, a click on a tile next to it slides that one into it; get 1 through 15 in reading order with the gap last and it says so.

    arrows / hjkl   slide the gap    click   slide the tile next to it     n               new game
apps/puzzle.author: Omar Sakka

apps/quran.title: Quran
apps/quran.about:
The Quran in Arabic, with tashkeel, to read, search and hear

the Quran in a window, in Arabic only and with every mark of tashkeel, laid out a word at a time so that a word can be heard: click it for that word, enter for the ayah, s for the sura from there on.

The text is read from Quran.com's public API once, on first use, by a job in the background, and kept as plain files under ~/.local/share/hibr/quran/ -- after that the Quran reads and searches offline, and only the sound needs the network. Nothing is translated: the window draws the Quran in Arabic whatever language the desktop speaks. Words are the API's own, each with the number of the clip the word-by-word recitation (audio.qurancdn.com) holds for it -- a word and the sign of stopping after it are one word here, as they are there. An ayah's recitation is everyayah.com's, in the reciter chosen on the Reciter menu.
apps/quran.author: Omar Sakka
apps/quran.name: quran

apps/clock.title: Clock
apps/clock.about:
The time and the date

the time, large, and the date under it.

It only draws, so it can never take a key meant for another window.
apps/clock.author: Omar Sakka
apps/clock.name: clock

apps/prayer.title: Prayer Times
apps/prayer.about:
Today's prayer times for where you are, the next one lit

a desk accessory (Gitea #70): today's times for where the person is, by the method chosen in Control Panel > Prayer Times, the next one lit with how long until it. The times come from wm/prayer.hibr's dt_ptimes, so the window, the bar and the notes always agree.
apps/prayer.author: Omar Sakka
apps/prayer.name: prayer

apps/mines.title: Mines
apps/mines.about:
Clear the field without stepping on anything.

The board is three strings of one character per cell: where the mines are, how many touch each cell, and what the player has seen.  A cell is read with ${s:i:1} and written by slicing around it, and opening an empty region is a loop over a stack of indices, so there is no recursion to run out of and nothing here is not ordinary shell.
apps/mines.author: Omar Sakka
apps/mines.name: mines

apps/snake.title: Snake
apps/snake.about:
Eat, grow, and do not bite yourself.

The snake is a string of "row,col" cells, head first.  A step puts a new head on the front and, unless it has just eaten, takes the tail off the back; running into itself is a pattern match on that string.  No arrays, no C: a game written in the shell, stepping on $EPOCHREALTIME.
apps/snake.author: Omar Sakka
apps/snake.name: snake

apps/bricks.title: Bricks
apps/bricks.about:
Knock the wall down

a bat, a ball and a wall to knock down, after Arkanoid.

Each row of the wall is a string of 1s and 0s, one per brick.  The ball moves one row and one or two columns a step, and takes the columns one at a time, so it never passes through the corner of a brick.  Where it lands on the bat decides how steeply it leaves: the ends send it off at a slant, and the middle sends it back the way it came.
apps/bricks.author: Omar Sakka
apps/bricks.name: bricks

apps/boxer.title: Boxer
apps/boxer.about:
DOS games, one folder to a game, in the way Boxer keeps them on a Mac. A game lives in a folder of its own, NAME.boxer, holding the game's drive C, its box art (.cover.png), the person's DOSBox settings and the game's saves. The games folder is ~/Dos Games, and Control Panel > Boxer (or BX_SHELF) names another. Files shows the folders, and a double click on one plays it, in a window of its own (boxerplay); a right click offers Get Info, where the program, sound card, MIDI, graphics and the game's name are set.

This window is for getting a game in. Drop a folder, a zip, a disc image or a program on it, or choose one with Import, and it is made into a NAME.boxer the way Boxer does it: an installer is run first, from the game's disc as D:.
apps/boxer.author: Omar Sakka
apps/boxer.name: boxer

apps/mail.title: Mail
apps/mail.about:
Email, offline, labels and conversations as Gmail has them

email in a window, laid out as Gmail lays it out: a search bar, the labels down the side with their unread counts, the conversations in a list -- the sender, the subject and a snippet, the date -- and a conversation opened in place, each message's text drawn from its HTML by the html module, its attached pictures by the img module. Gmail's keys work: j and k move, o or enter opens, u goes back, e archives, # deletes, s stars, I and U mark read and unread, l labels, v moves, c composes, r and a reply and reply to all, f forwards, / searches, and g then i, s, t, d or a goes to the inbox, starred, sent, drafts or all mail.

Everything is kept offline, per account, under ~/.local/share/hibr/mail/ACCOUNT -- msgs.db and the messages themselves -- by lib/mailsync.hibr, run in the background; a second job waits in IMAP IDLE and starts a sync the moment something arrives. What is done here is done to the copy at once and queued for the server, which the next sync brings it to. Accounts are the email module's (~/.config/hibr/mail, readable only by you), set up in Control Panel > Mail; a Google account uses an app password.
apps/mail.author: Omar Sakka
apps/mail.name: mail

apps/youtube.title: YouTube
apps/youtube.about:
YouTube, in a window

YouTube in a window: search, playlists and channels, the picture drawn as cells and the sound through the machine's own device, with a history that takes a video up where it was left, and favourites.

Nothing here is a YouTube client of its own. YouTube's own page runs in the web module's engine, and what the engine can do is its `web caps`. With WebKit (hibr-browser) the engine fetches, decodes and plays the video itself, picture and sound, as it does any page's; the page is drawn here as cells or pixels with YouTube's own controls set aside. With Chromium the page's player fetches the video at the lowest quality, muted, and the web module's tap copies every chunk it hands the browser's media source down two pipes into a media player, which decodes them with FFmpeg's libraries and plays them here. Either way this app drives YouTube's player: play and pause, a time, the volume. A search, a playlist or a channel is read from the page's own data.
apps/youtube.author: Omar Sakka
apps/youtube.name: youtube

apps/browser.title: Browser
apps/browser.about:
The web, in a window: a browser engine driven by the web module (a headless Chromium, or WPE WebKit from hibr-browser), each page drawn as cells -- its text where the browser laid it out, in its colours, over a half-block picture of its backgrounds and images. Links are followed with a click, fields typed into, pages scrolled with the wheel or the page keys.

A tab strip along the top -- a click switches, x closes, + opens another -- then back, forward, reload and the address: what is typed there is gone to as it is, with https:// put in front of a bare name, or searched for when it is not an address at all (BW_SEARCH). f6 or ctrl-l puts the keyboard in it; enter goes, escape gives it back to the page. Every other key goes to the page, except one the desktop holds.
apps/browser.author: Omar Sakka
apps/browser.name: browser

apps/pdfr.title: PDF Reader
apps/pdfr.about:
A PDF reader: pages as pictures where the terminal can, text where it cannot

a PDF reader (Gitea #348). The pages are drawn by the pdf module, which renders through Poppler loaded at run time, and placed by the img module, so a page is pixels on a terminal that takes them, half blocks or characters on one that does not, and -- under View > Text, or with no img at all -- the page's own text, wrapped to the window.

The document is one continuous column of pages: the wheel, the arrows, page up and down and the scroll bar move through it, and a view that spans the foot of one page and the head of the next is one picture. Fit Width is where a document opens; Fit Page, and zoom in and out, are on the View menu and on w, f, + and -. / searches the whole document, n and N step through what it found, each marked on its page. o shows the contents beside the pages; a link on a page is followed by clicking it -- to its page, or an address to the Browser. A drag selects text, and Copy takes it (or the whole page when nothing is selected); g goes to a page.
apps/pdfr.author: Omar Sakka
apps/pdfr.name: pdfr

apps/diagram.title: Diagram
apps/diagram.about:
A Mermaid diagram editor: the text, and the diagram

a Mermaid diagram editor: the text on one side, the drawing on the other, each following the other as it changes.

The editor half is widgets/textarea.hibr as it comes -- a buffer, a cursor, a selection, undo and the clipboard -- and the drawing half is mods/mermaid, which answers with the text of every row and the style of every character in it as runs. widgets/putruns.hibr draws those with a pen a letter, so the diagram is in the window's own theme colours and nothing here parses an escape sequence. See mods/mermaid/README.md for the three kinds of diagram this understands and what it says plainly that it does not.
apps/diagram.author: Omar Sakka
apps/diagram.name: diagram

apps/sheet.title: Sheet
apps/sheet.about:
A spreadsheet whose formulas are hibr.

What this comment says is now a page as well -- docs/sheet.md -- because for twenty releases it was the *only* place any of it was written down, and nobody using the app was ever going to read a source file. apps/dbase.name: dbase

apps/write.title: Write
apps/write.about:
A word processor for markdown, shown as it reads

a word processor for markdown, after MacWrite: what you write is shown as it will read -- headings large, bold bold, italic italic, lists with their bullets, quotes with their bar, code shaded, links underlined, rules drawn -- and only the line the cursor is on shows its markdown, the marks dimmed, so it can always be edited exactly. The toolbar and the Format menu put the marks in for you: on the selection, or on the line.

A .txt file -- or anything that is not markdown -- is edited as plain text, wrapped, nothing rendered. Files are opened from Files (Write is what .md and .txt open in), with File > Open…, or dropped on the window; File > Save writes the file (ctrl-s, settable as Save), Save As… asks where. A window with unsaved changes asks before it closes, and keeps them across Restart Desktop.

system/screenshot.title: Screenshot…
system/screenshot.about:
Take a screenshot of the screen, a window or an area

the desk accessory that takes one: Screenshot… asks Screen, Window or Area, the same as its shortcut (wm/shot.hibr does the taking). It opens no window of its own, so it gives screenshot_launch and nothing else; the Image Viewer, beside it, is what shows an .ans one afterwards.
system/screenshot.author: Omar Sakka
system/screenshot.name: screenshot

system/modman.title: Modules
system/modman.about:
What this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either

Modules: what this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either (#133).

Everything here is `mod avail`'s own answer: it walks the module path and reads each object's descriptor *without calling its init*, so a module can be named, versioned and described before it is ever loaded. In a pipe that answer is one line of eight tab-separated fields per module, which is what this reads -- never the column form, which is for a person.
system/modman.author: Omar Sakka
system/modman.name: modman

system/about.title: About This Computer
system/about.about:
About this computer: the machine, and the desktop running on it

what this is, and what it is running on.

On Linux the machine's own numbers come from /proc, read directly and costing no fork, the same way mods/sysinfo does in C. Nothing else keeps a /proc, so everywhere else forks a system command instead -- vm_stat and sysctl for memory, top for CPU, both throttled to AB_SLOWMS since forking a command every frame is not something to do at DT_TICK's pace. A window rather than the one-line note it used to be, because a bar that means something has to keep being redrawn, and a note fades on its own.
system/about.author: Omar Sakka
system/about.name: about

system/clipboard.title: Clipboard
system/clipboard.about:
The clipboard's history: copy something back, pin it, keep it

the clipboard's history, newest first (wm/clip.hibr keeps it). Each line is when it was copied, a ★ if pinned, a • on what is on the clipboard now, and the start of the text. Enter makes the selected one the clipboard again; p pins it, so it is never dropped; delete takes it away. A paste into this window -- alt-v, or the machine's own -- keeps what was pasted, to come back to later; Copy takes the selected one.
system/clipboard.author: Omar Sakka
system/clipboard.name: clipboard

system/tasks.title: Task Manager
system/tasks.about:
What is running, and a way to end one of them.

On Linux, reads /proc directly, the same technique mods/mon and the about window both use: no forking, and no dependency on anything but the kernel giving a truthful /proc. Elsewhere, one ps -axo per scan, since there is no /proc to read there at all -- ps already computes %CPU itself, so there is no delta of its own to keep between scans, unlike the Linux path. Sorted by CPU or memory, x or Task > End Task sends the selected one SIGTERM, shift-x sends SIGKILL.
system/tasks.author: Omar Sakka
system/tasks.name: tasks

system/notifications.title: Notifications
system/notifications.about:
A read-only look back at recent notifications

a look back at what DT_NOTEHIST kept: newest first, each note's time, priority, sender and text. Up and down select one, delete clears it, and the History menu clears the low ones or all of them.

Opened directly by the menu bar's icon (dt_bar in wm/bar.hibr, dt_mouse in wm/input.hibr) and by the Notifications pane's own "View History" row, never from a generic Applications pick -- hidden, the same reason About and Process Details are: nothing about "show me what already happened" makes sense launched with no history behind it, though here an empty one just shows an empty list rather than being refused.
system/notifications.author: Omar Sakka
system/notifications.name: notifications

system/catalogue.title: Catalogue
system/catalogue.about:
The application catalogue: browse, install, update and remove

Applications: the catalogue in a window. `apps` is the whole implementation and this is a window around it, the way the Vault accessory is a window around `vw` -- anything one can do the other can, because there is only one of them (Gitea #219).

It reads `apps -j`, never the columns `apps` prints for a person: the command answers JSON for exactly this, so the window and the command read one answer instead of one parsing the other's layout. Parsing a layout is how a window comes to disagree with its own command.
system/catalogue.author: Omar Sakka
system/catalogue.name: catalogue

control-panel/aboutme.title: About Me
control-panel/aboutme.about: The Control Panel pane for About Me: the name, the line under it and the picture the login screen shows for you (programs/desktop/login/), and which session it starts. They live in ~/.config/hibr/me.json -- data, never run, since the login screen reads it before anyone has logged in (as you, never as root). The picture is a PNG or JPEG anywhere you can read it; the file keeps its path.
control-panel/aboutme.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/aboutme.name: aboutme

control-panel/displays.title: Displays
control-panel/displays.about: Control Panel's own picture of a multi-monitor arrangement: a dropdown to choose which display is primary, and every attached display drawn to scale below it from hold clients, dragged to reposition (hold move on release). Right-click a rectangle for Detach (hold drop) or Identify (flash its own name on its own screen, so whoever is looking can tell which is which). The primary display is the picture's own anchor -- every rectangle is positioned relative to it, so switching which one is primary, or dragging a *different* display, never moves where the primary itself draws -- but its own rectangle cannot be dragged: the dropdown is the one reliable way to change it, since a mouse click precise enough to land on a specific terminal cell with *no* movement at all is not something to depend on, over ssh least of all. Nothing else is kept that a fresh read of hold clients cannot recompute -- the same as every other pane's row list is rebuilt every frame -- except the drag itself, which is this window's own gesture in progress and belongs nowhere else, and is frozen against hold clients while it is happening: re-reading mid-drag would have the dragged rectangle's own base position shift under the live preview the moment the release this same drag ends in reaches the server.
control-panel/displays.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/displays.name: displays

control-panel/shortcuts.title: Shortcuts
control-panel/shortcuts.about: The Control Panel pane for every shortcut in one list: the desktop's own actions, then a launch shortcut for any app. Activating a row captures its next key; the ✕ beside a key, or delete or backspace on its row, clears it. wm/keys.hibr does all of it -- including asking before taking a key another action has. Every key the desktop acts on is here, the menu bar's, Copy's, Cut's and Paste's included. A key two actions share, which only a settings file edited by hand can arrange, is marked ⚠ on both. Above them all, Shortcut Key: which modifiers the desktop's own chords use (DT_MOD, Gitea #326) -- Alt, Super or Alt, or Super -- every row then showing what to press.
control-panel/shortcuts.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/shortcuts.name: shortcuts

control-panel/network.title: Servers
control-panel/network.about: The Control Panel pane for WebDAV servers (wm/remote.hibr): one row per server, each opening the dialog that changes it; Add Server; whether a remote file's copy is put back when it is saved; how long a server may take; and emptying the copies kept. Servers live in the dav module's own list, readable only by its owner -- this pane never shows a password.
control-panel/network.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/network.name: network

control-panel/pictures.title: Pictures
control-panel/pictures.about:
The Control Panel pane for how a picture is drawn: half blocks, the same in grey, the character ramp, or real pixels where the terminal can place them. One setting reaches every picture the desktop draws -- the Image Viewer, the wallpaper, Mail's pictures, the film player and the browser -- since each passes DT_IMGMODE to the module that draws it.

What the terminal can do is shown beside it, because the honest answer is "it depends on your terminal", and it names the protocol in force: the kitty graphics protocol or sixel, each needing the terminal to say what a cell measures (ADR 0037). Which of the two is not a choice -- no terminal does both well, and kitty does not do sixel at all -- so the setting says Pixels and the console picks.
control-panel/pictures.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/pictures.name: pictures

control-panel/networks.title: Network
control-panel/networks.about:
The Control Panel pane for the machine's network and Wi-Fi

the Control Panel pane called Network (Gitea #311): what the machine is on and its address, Wi-Fi on or off, the networks in reach to join, the ones it knows to forget, and the item on the menu bar. It acts through menubar/network.hibr, which says how this machine is networked: NetworkManager, or iproute2's view alone.

The pane is called networks, not network, on purpose: network is the WebDAV servers' pane (titled Servers), shipped and in the catalogue, and a copy of it installed in a person's own scope would win over a shipped file of the same name -- so a new pane there would be shadowed by an old one.
control-panel/networks.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/networks.name: networks

control-panel/desktop.title: Desktop
control-panel/desktop.about: The Control Panel pane for the bare desktop: which icons sit on it, how many workspaces it has, whether Cycle goes through this one's windows or every one's, how often a busy screen is redrawn, and how screenshots are taken and where they go.
control-panel/desktop.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/desktop.name: desktop

control-panel/mouse.title: Mouse
control-panel/mouse.about: The Control Panel pane for what the mouse does to a window: whether a plain side resizes it as well as a corner, whether a modifier click anywhere in its body moves it and which modifier, and what a double click on its title bar does, whether a dragged window follows by its outline or whole, how far one notch of the wheel scrolls, and whether and how soon a tooltip shows. wm/input.hibr reads the window settings and every scrolling window the wheel's; this pane only changes the DT_* settings.
control-panel/mouse.author: Omar Sakka
control-panel/mouse.name: mouse

control-panel/menubar.title: Menu Bar

X11 programs in windows (Gitea #290, #291): Firefox, GTK and Qt programs, and anything else that speaks X11, run on the desktop. Each window starts an Xvfb of its own, a virtual X server that draws the screen into a file it maps, and the xscr module maps the same file and puts the screen into the window -- as pixels where the terminal can place them, half blocks where it cannot. Keys, clicks, drags, the wheel and paste go to it through XTEST; the screen is drawn only when the server says it changed (DAMAGE), so an idle or hidden one costs nothing.

The programs are a list Control Panel > X Screen keeps -- a name, a command, how its window behaves and how it is drawn -- and each one is an entry under Applications > X Screen, opening a window titled for it and, once the program names its own window, `Name [its title]`. The app itself is hidden: an empty screen with nothing on it is nothing to choose.
xscreen.author: Omar Sakka
xscreen.name: xscreen

files.title: Files
files.about:
A file browser for the desktop, and a lister on its own.

    hibr programs/desktop/apps/files.hibr /etc
files.author: Omar Sakka
files.name: files

term.title: Terminal
term.about:
A shell in a window, which is the last step of decision 0020.

The window manager hands this app a rectangle and some keys; the term module runs a program on a pseudo terminal, keeps a picture of its screen and paints that picture into the rectangle. What runs inside is a real program with a real terminal: it edits its own line, draws its own colours and does not know it is in a window.
term.author: Omar Sakka
term.name: term

calendar.title: Calendar
calendar.about:
Your calendars, a month at a time, kept offline from CalDAV

your calendars, kept on this machine from a CalDAV server (Nextcloud, Fastmail, iCloud, Radicale, anything standard): a month at a time, each day's events in it, and the chosen day's events listed underneath; or an agenda of what is coming. The arrows choose a day, n and p (or page down and up) change month, t comes back to today, a and m switch to the agenda and back, tab moves between the month and the day's list, c makes an event on the chosen day, enter makes one there or edits the one chosen in the list, # removes it, R syncs now.

The servers are Contacts' -- Control Panel > PIM -- and lib/pimsync.hibr keeps their calendars under ~/.local/share/hibr/pim/SERVER: each event's file, and every occurrence from a year back to two years on, which this reads by date. A change made here is queued and sent at the next sync. Reminders go off whether or not a Calendar window is open: a ticker run after every frame looks for the next one and asks for the frame it is due in.
calendar.author: Omar Sakka
calendar.name: calendar

stickies.title: Stickies
stickies.about:
Notes stuck on the desktop, each its own colour

notes stuck on the desktop, as many as you like, each its own colour, each saved as you type. Launching Stickies opens every note there is (a first, empty one if there are none); the Note menu makes a new one, changes the colour, and deletes one. Closing a note only puts it away until Stickies is opened again -- it is still there.

The colours are the notes' own, not the theme's, the way a game's art is: a yellow note is yellow on every theme. Text wraps at the window's width, and the desktop's Edit menu works on it -- undo and redo, cut, copy, paste, select all.
stickies.author: Omar Sakka
stickies.name: stickies

imgview.title: Image Viewer
imgview.about: A picture in a window, drawn by the img module. Opens with a path (dt_launch imgview "$path", the same as any other app takes one through its own _open), or empty and waiting for one dropped onto it from a file browser -- there is no file-open dialog anywhere in this desktop, so a drop is the only way in short of already knowing the path.
imgview.author: Omar Sakka
imgview.name: imgview

calc.title: Calculator
calc.about:
A calculator for the desktop, and a program on its own.

Sourced by a session it is an app: the window manager finds calc_draw, calc_key and calc_click and calls those.  Run directly it evaluates its arguments and prints the answer, so it is useful without a desktop:
calc.author: Omar Sakka
calc.name: calc

puzzle.title: Puzzle
puzzle.about:
The sliding tile puzzle, 15 numbered tiles and one gap in a 4x4 frame. Arrows move the gap, a click on a tile next to it slides that one into it; get 1 through 15 in reading order with the gap last and it says so.

    arrows / hjkl   slide the gap    click   slide the tile next to it     n               new game
puzzle.author: Omar Sakka
puzzle.name: puzzle

quran.title: Quran
quran.about:
The Quran in Arabic, with tashkeel, to read, search and hear

the Quran in a window, in Arabic only and with every mark of tashkeel, laid out a word at a time so that a word can be heard: click it for that word, enter for the ayah, s for the sura from there on.

The text is read from Quran.com's public API once, on first use, by a job in the background, and kept as plain files under ~/.local/share/hibr/quran/ -- after that the Quran reads and searches offline, and only the sound needs the network. Nothing is translated: the window draws the Quran in Arabic whatever language the desktop speaks. Words are the API's own, each with the number of the clip the word-by-word recitation (audio.qurancdn.com) holds for it -- a word and the sign of stopping after it are one word here, as they are there. An ayah's recitation is everyayah.com's, in the reciter chosen on the Reciter menu.
quran.author: Omar Sakka
quran.name: quran

prayer.title: Prayer Times
prayer.about:
Today's prayer times for where you are, the next one lit

a desk accessory (Gitea #70): today's times for where the person is, by the method chosen in Control Panel > Prayer Times, the next one lit with how long until it. The times come from wm/prayer.hibr's dt_ptimes, so the window, the bar and the notes always agree.
prayer.author: Omar Sakka
prayer.name: prayer

mines.title: Mines
mines.about:
Clear the field without stepping on anything.

The board is three strings of one character per cell: where the mines are, how many touch each cell, and what the player has seen.  A cell is read with ${s:i:1} and written by slicing around it, and opening an empty region is a loop over a stack of indices, so there is no recursion to run out of and nothing here is not ordinary shell.
mines.author: Omar Sakka
mines.name: mines

snake.title: Snake
snake.about:
Eat, grow, and do not bite yourself.

The snake is a string of "row,col" cells, head first.  A step puts a new head on the front and, unless it has just eaten, takes the tail off the back; running into itself is a pattern match on that string.  No arrays, no C: a game written in the shell, stepping on $EPOCHREALTIME.
snake.author: Omar Sakka
snake.name: snake

bricks.title: Bricks
bricks.about:
Knock the wall down

a bat, a ball and a wall to knock down, after Arkanoid.

Each row of the wall is a string of 1s and 0s, one per brick.  The ball moves one row and one or two columns a step, and takes the columns one at a time, so it never passes through the corner of a brick.  Where it lands on the bat decides how steeply it leaves: the ends send it off at a slant, and the middle sends it back the way it came.
bricks.author: Omar Sakka
bricks.name: bricks

boxer.title: Boxer
boxer.about:
DOS games, one folder to a game, in the way Boxer keeps them on a Mac. A game lives in a folder of its own, NAME.boxer, holding the game's drive C, its box art (.cover.png), the person's DOSBox settings and the game's saves. The games folder is ~/Dos Games, and Control Panel > Boxer (or BX_SHELF) names another. Files shows the folders, and a double click on one plays it, in a window of its own (boxerplay); a right click offers Get Info, where the program, sound card, MIDI, graphics and the game's name are set.

This window is for getting a game in. Drop a folder, a zip, a disc image or a program on it, or choose one with Import, and it is made into a NAME.boxer the way Boxer does it: an installer is run first, from the game's disc as D:.
boxer.author: Omar Sakka
boxer.name: boxer

mail.title: Mail
mail.about:
Email, offline, labels and conversations as Gmail has them

email in a window, laid out as Gmail lays it out: a search bar, the labels down the side with their unread counts, the conversations in a list -- the sender, the subject and a snippet, the date -- and a conversation opened in place, each message's text drawn from its HTML by the html module, its attached pictures by the img module. Gmail's keys work: j and k move, o or enter opens, u goes back, e archives, # deletes, s stars, I and U mark read and unread, l labels, v moves, c composes, r and a reply and reply to all, f forwards, / searches, and g then i, s, t, d or a goes to the inbox, starred, sent, drafts or all mail.

Everything is kept offline, per account, under ~/.local/share/hibr/mail/ACCOUNT -- msgs.db and the messages themselves -- by lib/mailsync.hibr, run in the background; a second job waits in IMAP IDLE and starts a sync the moment something arrives. What is done here is done to the copy at once and queued for the server, which the next sync brings it to. Accounts are the email module's (~/.config/hibr/mail, readable only by you), set up in Control Panel > Mail; a Google account uses an app password.
mail.author: Omar Sakka
mail.name: mail

youtube.title: YouTube
youtube.about:
YouTube, in a window

YouTube in a window: search, playlists and channels, the picture drawn as cells and the sound through the machine's own device, with a history that takes a video up where it was left, and favourites.

Nothing here is a YouTube client of its own. YouTube's own page runs in the web module's engine, and what the engine can do is its `web caps`. With WebKit (hibr-browser) the engine fetches, decodes and plays the video itself, picture and sound, as it does any page's; the page is drawn here as cells or pixels with YouTube's own controls set aside. With Chromium the page's player fetches the video at the lowest quality, muted, and the web module's tap copies every chunk it hands the browser's media source down two pipes into a media player, which decodes them with FFmpeg's libraries and plays them here. Either way this app drives YouTube's player: play and pause, a time, the volume. A search, a playlist or a channel is read from the page's own data.
youtube.author: Omar Sakka
youtube.name: youtube

browser.title: Browser
browser.about:
The web, in a window: a browser engine driven by the web module (a headless Chromium, or WPE WebKit from hibr-browser), each page drawn as cells -- its text where the browser laid it out, in its colours, over a half-block picture of its backgrounds and images. Links are followed with a click, fields typed into, pages scrolled with the wheel or the page keys.

A tab strip along the top -- a click switches, x closes, + opens another -- then back, forward, reload and the address: what is typed there is gone to as it is, with https:// put in front of a bare name, or searched for when it is not an address at all (BW_SEARCH). f6 or ctrl-l puts the keyboard in it; enter goes, escape gives it back to the page. Every other key goes to the page, except one the desktop holds.
browser.author: Omar Sakka
browser.name: browser

pdfr.title: PDF Reader
pdfr.about:
A PDF reader: pages as pictures where the terminal can, text where it cannot

a PDF reader (Gitea #348). The pages are drawn by the pdf module, which renders through Poppler loaded at run time, and placed by the img module, so a page is pixels on a terminal that takes them, half blocks or characters on one that does not, and -- under View > Text, or with no img at all -- the page's own text, wrapped to the window.

The document is one continuous column of pages: the wheel, the arrows, page up and down and the scroll bar move through it, and a view that spans the foot of one page and the head of the next is one picture. Fit Width is where a document opens; Fit Page, and zoom in and out, are on the View menu and on w, f, + and -. / searches the whole document, n and N step through what it found, each marked on its page. o shows the contents beside the pages; a link on a page is followed by clicking it -- to its page, or an address to the Browser. A drag selects text, and Copy takes it (or the whole page when nothing is selected); g goes to a page.
pdfr.author: Omar Sakka
pdfr.name: pdfr

diagram.title: Diagram
diagram.about:
A Mermaid diagram editor: the text, and the diagram

a Mermaid diagram editor: the text on one side, the drawing on the other, each following the other as it changes.

The editor half is widgets/textarea.hibr as it comes -- a buffer, a cursor, a selection, undo and the clipboard -- and the drawing half is mods/mermaid, which answers with the text of every row and the style of every character in it as runs. widgets/putruns.hibr draws those with a pen a letter, so the diagram is in the window's own theme colours and nothing here parses an escape sequence. See mods/mermaid/README.md for the three kinds of diagram this understands and what it says plainly that it does not.
diagram.author: Omar Sakka
diagram.name: diagram

sheet.title: Sheet
sheet.about:
A spreadsheet whose formulas are hibr.

What this comment says is now a page as well -- docs/sheet.md -- because for twenty releases it was the *only* place any of it was written down, and nobody using the app was ever going to read a source file. Reported as "I have no idea how to use it this way ... there are no examples either" (Gitea #150). The app itself says it too: the formula bar shows what a formula looks like on an empty cell, Help > How Formulas Work is a page of it, and Help > Open the Tour is a sheet of worked examples with one cell the sandbox refuses, which is the only way to see what it does. Keep the three in step: this comment, that page, and the Help window.
sheet.author: Omar Sakka
sheet.name: sheet

dbase.title: dBASE
dbase.about:
A little dBASE III: dot prompt, BROWSE, APPEND

a little dBASE III, on the db module: the dot prompt, BROWSE, an APPEND form, and System 7 style menus driving the same commands.

  . CREATE stats          fields asked for one at a time, as below   . USE stats   . APPEND                a form: tab or enter between fields, escape out   . LIST FOR load > 2.5 .AND. host = 'web1'   . COUNT FOR host = 'web1'   . SUM load    . AVERAGE load FOR host = 'web2'   . BROWSE                arrows and page keys, escape back   . DISPLAY STRUCTURE     . DIR     . ? RECCOUNT()     . HELP     . QUIT
dbase.author: Omar Sakka
dbase.name: dbase

write.title: Write
write.about:
A word processor for markdown, shown as it reads

a word processor for markdown, after MacWrite: what you write is shown as it will read -- headings large, bold bold, italic italic, lists with their bullets, quotes with their bar, code shaded, links underlined, rules drawn -- and only the line the cursor is on shows its markdown, the marks dimmed, so it can always be edited exactly. The toolbar and the Format menu put the marks in for you: on the selection, or on the line.

A .txt file -- or anything that is not markdown -- is edited as plain text, wrapped, nothing rendered. Files are opened from Files (Write is what .md and .txt open in), with File > Open…, or dropped on the window; File > Save writes the file (ctrl-s, settable as Save), Save As… asks where. A window with unsaved changes asks before it closes, and keeps them across Restart Desktop.
write.author: Omar Sakka
write.name: write

screenshot.title: Screenshot…
screenshot.about:
Take a screenshot of the screen, a window or an area

the desk accessory that takes one: Screenshot… asks Screen, Window or Area, the same as its shortcut (wm/shot.hibr does the taking). It opens no window of its own, so it gives screenshot_launch and nothing else; the Image Viewer, beside it, is what shows an .ans one afterwards.
screenshot.author: Omar Sakka
screenshot.name: screenshot

modman.title: Modules
modman.about:
What this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either

Modules: what this shell can load, what it has loaded, and a way to change either (#133).

Everything here is `mod avail`'s own answer: it walks the module path and reads each object's descriptor *without calling its init*, so a module can be named, versioned and described before it is ever loaded. In a pipe that answer is one line of eight tab-separated fields per module, which is what this reads -- never the column form, which is for a person.
modman.author: Omar Sakka
modman.name: modman

about.title: About This Computer
about.about:
About this computer: the machine, and the desktop running on it

what this is, and what it is running on.

On Linux the machine's own numbers come from /proc, read directly and costing no fork, the same way mods/sysinfo does in C. Nothing else keeps a /proc, so everywhere else forks a system command instead -- vm_stat and sysctl for memory, top for CPU, both throttled to AB_SLOWMS since forking a command every frame is not something to do at DT_TICK's pace. A window rather than the one-line note it used to be, because a bar that means something has to keep being redrawn, and a note fades on its own.
about.author: Omar Sakka
about.name: about

clipboard.title: Clipboard
clipboard.about:
The clipboard's history: copy something back, pin it, keep it

the clipboard's history, newest first (wm/clip.hibr keeps it). Each line is when it was copied, a ★ if pinned, a • on what is on the clipboard now, and the start of the text. Enter makes the selected one the clipboard again; p pins it, so it is never dropped; delete takes it away. A paste into this window -- alt-v, or the machine's own -- keeps what was pasted, to come back to later; Copy takes the selected one.
clipboard.author: Omar Sakka
clipboard.name: clipboard

tasks.title: Task Manager
tasks.about:
What is running, and a way to end one of them.

On Linux, reads /proc directly, the same technique mods/mon and the about window both use: no forking, and no dependency on anything but the kernel giving a truthful /proc. Elsewhere, one ps -axo per scan, since there is no /proc to read there at all -- ps already computes %CPU itself, so there is no delta of its own to keep between scans, unlike the Linux path. Sorted by CPU or memory, x or Task > End Task sends the selected one SIGTERM, shift-x sends SIGKILL.
tasks.author: Omar Sakka
tasks.name: tasks

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.about:
A read-only look back at recent notifications

a look back at what DT_NOTEHIST kept: newest first, each note's time, priority, sender and text. Up and down select one, delete clears it, and the History menu clears the low ones or all of them.

Opened directly by the menu bar's icon (dt_bar in wm/bar.hibr, dt_mouse in wm/input.hibr) and by the Notifications pane's own "View History" row, never from a generic Applications pick -- hidden, the same reason About and Process Details are: nothing about "show me what already happened" makes sense launched with no history behind it, though here an empty one just shows an empty list rather than being refused.
notifications.author: Omar Sakka
notifications.name: notifications

catalogue.title: Catalogue
catalogue.about:
The application catalogue: browse, install, update and remove

Applications: the catalogue in a window. `apps` is the whole implementation and this is a window around it, the way the Vault accessory is a window around `vw` -- anything one can do the other can, because there is only one of them (Gitea #219).

It reads `apps -j`, never the columns `apps` prints for a person: the command answers JSON for exactly this, so the window and the command read one answer instead of one parsing the other's layout. Parsing a layout is how a window comes to disagree with its own command.
catalogue.author: Omar Sakka
catalogue.name: catalogue

aboutme.title: About Me
aboutme.about: The Control Panel pane for About Me: the name, the line under it and the picture the login screen shows for you (programs/desktop/login/), and which session it starts. They live in ~/.config/hibr/me.json -- data, never run, since the login screen reads it before anyone has logged in (as you, never as root). The picture is a PNG or JPEG anywhere you can read it; the file keeps its path.
aboutme.author: Omar Sakka
aboutme.name: aboutme

displays.title: Displays
displays.about: Control Panel's own picture of a multi-monitor arrangement: a dropdown to choose which display is primary, and every attached display drawn to scale below it from hold clients, dragged to reposition (hold move on release). Right-click a rectangle for Detach (hold drop) or Identify (flash its own name on its own screen, so whoever is looking can tell which is which). The primary display is the picture's own anchor -- every rectangle is positioned relative to it, so switching which one is primary, or dragging a *different* display, never moves where the primary itself draws -- but its own rectangle cannot be dragged: the dropdown is the one reliable way to change it, since a mouse click precise enough to land on a specific terminal cell with *no* movement at all is not something to depend on, over ssh least of all. Nothing else is kept that a fresh read of hold clients cannot recompute -- the same as every other pane's row list is rebuilt every frame -- except the drag itself, which is this window's own gesture in progress and belongs nowhere else, and is frozen against hold clients while it is happening: re-reading mid-drag would have the dragged rectangle's own base position shift under the live preview the moment the release this same drag ends in reaches the server.
displays.author: Omar Sakka
displays.name: displays

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts
shortcuts.about: The Control Panel pane for every shortcut in one list: the desktop's own actions, then a launch shortcut for any app. Activating a row captures its next key; the ✕ beside a key, or delete or backspace on its row, clears it. wm/keys.hibr does all of it -- including asking before taking a key another action has. Every key the desktop acts on is here, the menu bar's, Copy's, Cut's and Paste's included. A key two actions share, which only a settings file edited by hand can arrange, is marked ⚠ on both. Above them all, Shortcut Key: which modifiers the desktop's own chords use (DT_MOD, Gitea #326) -- Alt, Super or Alt, or Super -- every row then showing what to press.
shortcuts.author: Omar Sakka
shortcuts.name: shortcuts

pictures.title: Pictures
pictures.about:
The Control Panel pane for how a picture is drawn: half blocks, the same in grey, the character ramp, or real pixels where the terminal can place them. One setting reaches every picture the desktop draws -- the Image Viewer, the wallpaper, Mail's pictures, the film player and the browser -- since each passes DT_IMGMODE to the module that draws it.

What the terminal can do is shown beside it, because the honest answer is "it depends on your terminal", and it names the protocol in force: the kitty graphics protocol or sixel, each needing the terminal to say what a cell measures (ADR 0037). Which of the two is not a choice -- no terminal does both well, and kitty does not do sixel at all -- so the setting says Pixels and the console picks.
pictures.author: Omar Sakka
pictures.name: pictures

networks.title: Network
networks.about:
The Control Panel pane for the machine's network and Wi-Fi

the Control Panel pane called Network (Gitea #311): what the machine is on and its address, Wi-Fi on or off, the networks in reach to join, the ones it knows to forget, and the item on the menu bar. It acts through menubar/network.hibr, which says how this machine is networked: NetworkManager, or iproute2's view alone.

The pane is called networks, not network, on purpose: network is the WebDAV servers' pane (titled Servers), shipped and in the catalogue, and a copy of it installed in a person's own scope would win over a shipped file of the same name -- so a new pane there would be shadowed by an old one.
networks.author: Omar Sakka
networks.name: networks

desktop.title: Desktop
desktop.about: The Control Panel pane for the bare desktop: which icons sit on it, how many workspaces it has, whether Cycle goes through this one's windows or every one's, how often a busy screen is redrawn, and how screenshots are taken and where they go.
desktop.author: Omar Sakka
desktop.name: desktop

mouse.title: Mouse
mouse.about: The Control Panel pane for what the mouse does to a window: whether a plain side resizes it as well as a corner, whether a modifier click anywhere in its body moves it and which modifier, and what a double click on its title bar does, whether a dragged window follows by its outline or whole, how far one notch of the wheel scrolls, and whether and how soon a tooltip shows. wm/input.hibr reads the window settings and every scrolling window the wheel's; this pane only changes the DT_* settings.
mouse.author: Omar Sakka
mouse.name: mouse

menubar.title: Menu Bar
menubar.about:
The Control Panel pane for the menu bar: how it looks -- the gap between its items, how much of a picture shows through it, the notification icon, its shadow, bold titles and how wide a menu may grow -- and what is on it, Menu Bar Items, every item on its right ticked on or off and dragged into the order it reads in (Gitea #396). These were Appearance's own Menu Bar rows until 0.99.356; the settings are the same ones, so nothing saved moves.

The pane is called barset, not menubar: dt_menubar is the window manager's own loader, and a pane's name is the prefix its callbacks are looked up by.
menubar.author: Omar Sakka
menubar.name: menubar

windows.title: Windows
windows.about:
The Control Panel pane for how a window looks and where it opens

the Control Panel pane for how a window looks and where a new one goes: its frame, which side its buttons dock to, where its title sits, which glyphs the buttons are drawn with, Placement, what Zoom fills -- the window's own display or every display (Gitea #286) -- and how wide a tiled workspace's main window is. How the mouse moves, resizes and double-clicks one is the Mouse pane's. Every value here is read by wm/frame.hibr; this pane only ever changes the DT_* settings, never the drawing itself.
windows.author: Omar Sakka
windows.name: windows

datetime.title: Date & Time
datetime.about:
The Control Panel pane for the time, the date and the time zone

the Control Panel pane for the time, the date, and a small world map with a mark near the machine's own time zone, System 7's Date & Time control panel. A custom pane, since a map needs a body of its own rather than two columns of text.

The map data, its scoring, and the zone1970.tab lookup are all copied from examples/traceroute.hibr rather than redone: CLAUDE.md's own trap about that map says not to adjust one by eye, and the same is true of drawing a second one. What is copied is copied unchanged; only the projection's target size differs, since this map is a corner of a settings pane and not a full screen.
datetime.author: Omar Sakka
datetime.name: datetime

filetypes.title: File Types
filetypes.about:
Which program opens which kind of file

the Control Panel pane for dt_handler's own extension-to- program table (DT_HANDLERS). Files' own Open With menu already reads it; this is where a mapping is added, changed or removed, rather than only through a dt_handler line in a script of your own -- which still works exactly as before, and is what dt_save now writes these back out as.
filetypes.author: Omar Sakka
filetypes.name: filetypes

appearance.title: Appearance
appearance.about: The Control Panel pane for how the desktop looks: the theme (the whole look at once), the colour scheme, the glyphs and trees, the shadows, and how dialog buttons look. The menu bar has a pane of its own since 0.99.356 (menubar.hibr, Gitea #396), its look and its items. The wallpaper has a pane of its own since 0.99.246 (wallset.hibr, Gitea #284), though a theme still carries one and applies it here. A theme or a colour scheme sets the variables the window manager already reads every frame, so a change shows on the next one, in every window at once.
appearance.author: Omar Sakka
appearance.name: appearance

versions.title: Versions
versions.about: Which image each part of this desktop is actually running. About This Computer cannot answer that: it draws $HIBR_VERSION, which is the *desktop process's* own version, and a restart replaces that process and every module it loads while leaving the hold server's image exactly as old as the session (Gitea #42, #198). Three states, asked and named separately, because they move independently.
versions.author: Omar Sakka
versions.name: versions

blit.title: Blit
blit.about:
API configuration and diagnostics for the Blit display server.

Auxiliary Apply changes the running policy; Save as Default writes Blit's existing settings resource with revision protection. Login preferences take effect at restart. Font changes use Blit's live-and-saved font API. Hibr Displays continues to own native desktop arrangement after initial attachment. Every network request is hibr's own dav request, in a bounded background job of the desktop's (dt_job); no curl, and the token never on a command line. The connection token is kept in a private user file, is masked in its editor, and is excluded from configuration exports. The privileged updater token is never requested. The source of this pane is this file, in the hibr catalogue (itdlabs/hibr-apps), not the Blit tree.
blit.author: Omar Sakka
blit.name: blit

wallset.title: Wallpaper
wallset.about:
The Control Panel pane for the wallpaper of each display

the Control Panel pane for the wallpaper: the pattern, or an image chosen in a picker of its own (control-panel/wallpaper.hibr), how it fills the screen, and how it is drawn -- for every display at once, or for one display by its name (Gitea #284). It was a section of Appearance until then; it is a pane of its own because a Display row choosing what every row below it applies to reads plainly here, and would not among Appearance's rows, which all apply everywhere.

A display is known by the name it attached under: --name if it was given one, otherwise the machine it connects from (dt_dispname), so a reattach finds it again. One with a wallpaper of its own keeps it in DT_WALLDIMG, DT_WALLDMODE and DT_WALLDPIC (wm/wallpaper.hibr); one with none follows All Displays, which is DT_WALLIMG, DT_WALLMODE and DT_WALLIMGMODE as before -- so a settings file written before this pane existed means exactly what it did. The pattern is one for the whole desktop, and is only offered under All Displays.
